title: How a grandma, an entrepreneur, and a product manager use AI
excerpt: We asked a group of disparate individuals what they ask AI chatbots about.

Senior Reporter

Rebecca Ruiz is a Senior Reporter at Mashable. She frequently covers mental health, digital culture, and technology. Her areas of expertise include suicide prevention, screen use and mental health, parenting, youth well-being, and meditation and mindfulness. Rebecca's experience prior to Mashable includes working as a staff writer, reporter, and editor at NBC News Digital and as a staff writer at Forbes. The majority of U.S. adults have used an artificial intelligence chatbot like Claude or ChatGPT, according to a recent YouGov survey commissioned by Mashable. We even know, generally speaking, how they view their chatbot in roles like assistant, tutor, consultant, therapist, and romantic partner — or all of the above. 

The nitty-gritty details of that use, however, are harder to grasp.

After all, people don't exactly go deep about their chatbot use with each other outside of social media platforms and Reddit forums. They might feel shame or stigma because they've turned a chatbot into their therapist or spouse. Or perhaps it's not fodder for conversation in the same way that Love Island takes over the group chat. 

So Mashable asked three very different people — a grandmother, an entrepreneur, and a technologist — how they use AI chatbots. 

Their answers reveal how a chatbot can become an essential utility for some people, even if they still grapple with the larger cultural shift artificial intelligence has wrought.

The grandma who knows what she wants from ChatGPT

Last fall, Barbara, 71, teamed up with her son and daughter-in-law to give ChatGPT a monumental task. They needed the large language model to help them understand whether Barbara's grandson, who has a learning disability, was achieving the learning goals set by his school district. 

Crucially, if the district answered this question affirmatively, they could argue Barbara's grandson no longer needed classroom support. She urgently felt he still did, and his parents agreed. 

"It seems like we were never getting a straight answer, and there were contradictory things being said," Barbara recounted to Mashable. She asked to go by her first name to protect her grandson's privacy.

The family trio turned to the chatbot for clarity amidst a brewing confrontation with school staff over the question. Barbara is a former educator and no stranger to the biannual meetings that typically determine whether a student receives classroom support, and to what extent. But even she felt overwhelmed by all the documentation her grandson had accumulated over years of elementary school. 

There were grades and test scores, of course. But her grandson's cognitive and intellectual abilities had also been tested by the district and medical professionals. They uploaded all of the paperwork and waited for ChatGPT to give its opinion. 

Via direct prompting, the model also considered the state's education disability law and regulations, as well as an uploaded copy of the Department of Education's Individuals with Disabilities Education Act handbook. ChatGPT ultimately sided with Barbara and her family. 

Barbara doesn't credit ChatGPT with returning a single smoking-gun finding or ironclad strategy. Instead, she said the chatbot's feedback made them feel better prepared for the discussion of her grandson's services. The family also hired an education advocate to help buttress their position. In the end, Barbara's grandson kept his classroom services. 

"It's amazing to me, and kind of disturbing, because I really try not to tell it a lot about myself."

Aside from this critical assignment, Barbara told Mashable she asks ChatGPT for practical recommendations or product comparisons. She had the chatbot create an itinerary for a summer trip to Ireland with friends; asked it to identify a dupe of a discontinued drugstore perfume that she loved; and requested its advice for $800 worth of car repairs proposed by her mechanic. ChatGPT said replenishing her Honda CRV's transmission and brake fluid was reasonable but to avoid, among other things, transmission flushes using high-pressure machines. 

The one thing Barbara avoids when engaging with ChatGPT? Talking to it like a friend or confidant, which she finds "creepy." 

Nonetheless, ChatGPT is fairly well acquainted with Barbara. 

"It's amazing to me, and kind of disturbing, because I really try not to tell it a lot about myself," she said. "I try to just keep it very effective, and it's still amazing how much it knows about me."

The AI anthropologist who runs teams of agents

Matt Artz is the type of AI user you may have read about in news articles or viral social media posts. He can command a team of Claude agents to do his bidding without constant supervision. In other words, he's living the life AI evangelists promise is possible for the rest of us in the not-so-distant future. 

But Artz is unique compared to many AI users. First of all, he can afford a $200 a month Max subscription to Claude, which gives him far more compute, or processing power, than free or lower-tier subscribers receive. As a result, he says he gets more work done in the same period of time. 

By day, he's an AI product manager. On his own time, Artz, who's in his mid-40s, is pursuing a Ph.D. in computational anthropology. 

It's no surprise then that Artz deploys agents to perform tasks like building a personal website based on a style guide he developed; reviewing and critiquing his academic work prior to submission; and backfilling a catalog of 200,00 anthropological journal articles so their bibliometric data appears in Wikidata. That last project he took on in his capacity as a board member of the American Anthropological Association. 

Mashable Light Speed

At the same time, Artz is clear-eyed about the limitations of large language models; he doesn't treat them as infallible.  

Because their output is probabilistic, models can approach the same task differently each time. That's why Artz is deliberate about giving agents detailed structure and direction for any assignment. Without that, an agent is potentially more likely to improvise in ways he didn't intend. He hasn't lost any data to an agent — yet. 

"It is not perfect," he told Mashable. "I don't think current agentic AI is yet suited for the highest order tasks that are super sensitive and have to be, you know, 100 percent accurate." 

Still, he notes that most knowledge work is subjective, which means there's rarely one "right" answer in the first place.

Artz uses AI like a normie, too. He's asked Claude to select a couch based on his living room arrangements and render how it would look in different colors. Artz uploaded years of sleep data and observations to Claude to optimize his shuteye. 

He says Claude helped pinpoint variables, including aspects of his bedtime routine from a journal he kept, that ultimately lengthened his deep sleep by about 20 minutes a night on average.

Artz is worried, though, that some AI users don't realize how much the output depends on their ability to question and push back on the model. Those who don't grasp that AI is probabilistic might not realize they can push back, rephrase a question, or prompt it from the opposite angle to see if an answer holds up.

Additionally, many people may not appreciate that additional compute can yield more sophisticated and reliable output. 

Artz says these factors have created an "intelligence divide."

"[H]ow much intelligence can you even pay for, right?" he asks.

In other words, even if everyone has access to an AI chatbot, the results will differ based on what model or subscription you can afford. 

The anti-tech entrepreneur

By Chase DiBenedetto

Larissa (Larz) May, 32, has a complex relationship with screens. 

She's a well-known digital wellness advocate, for one, an early pioneer of the "digital detox" movement, spurred by her own public reckoning with social media's mental health harms. 

She later founded #HalfTheStory, aimed at building better relationships between teens and technology. The nonprofit provides training, mentorship, and digital civics engagement programs for teens and schools, and puts young people at the center of the AI safety conversation, May explains. It facilitates analog gatherings like phone-free proms. May even collaborated with Hillary Clinton and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul on a teen-guided, phoneless school policy, with hopes of encouraging a nationwide shift away from screens. 

She's also the co-founder of Ginko, an AI-powered parenting tool that helps families build healthier digital habits and foster communication. The app, she says, turns screen time into a "springboard for the real world."

Here's the kicker: May may be a vocal critic of Big Tech, but she's definitely not a Luddite. 

"AI is an incredible sparring partner in the workplace."

"AI is an incredible sparring partner in the workplace," May says. She uses chatbots she thinks are less sycophantic, like Claude, to talk through ideas or fine-tune pitches. "I oftentimes say, 'Hey, pretend you are a really critical CMO and rip this apart.'" 

She also uses Granola, an AI note taker and meeting synthesizer, and Wispr Flow, an AI that lets her dictate her thoughts and turn them into text.

May says she understands why young people turn to chatbots for support. The post-COVID world has rendered many early career professionals and recent grads without workplace connection or mentorship. Widespread fatigue, exacerbated by conflict-filled newscycles and misinformation, make it easy to turn to an answer engine that can talk to you clearly and kindly. May finds herself leaning more on chatbots when she is feeling wiped out, too.

For many, social media feels like a stage requiring constant performance, she says. AI chatbots can appear as a more private space.

"Chatbots are like a green room," May explains. "AI is that soft corner that young people are going to because the world is very hard, and because we're going through so much change."

But May has first-hand experience with the negative side of tech, too. Chatbots, she says, cannot replace human capacity for invention, connection, and critical thinking. She sees vast potential for harm in how easy it is to become attached to AI and questions the motives of large tech companies. 

"Social media hacked our dopamine," says May. "But AI, in many ways, is hacking our oxytocin — the human connection hormone."

May still advocates for disconnecting, but that means something different in the age of AI.

"It is no longer about tech time. It is more about the times that you're not on tech," she advises. "In the way that 10 years ago I would say go on a social media fast one day a week, what's even more important now is to actually take one day a week and not use AI at work. See how much you're relying on it, so you know how much of your cognitive skills you might be losing."

If our careers, education, even our lives are like the cars we drive, she says, then we have to think of AI as a GPS. Chatbots provide pathways, ones you can ultimately choose not to take. They aren't the engines. 

"You should be in the driver's seat," May warns. "You should be telling AI who you want it to become, to critique what you're doing, instead of the other way around. If not, AI will drive you."

我们询问了一群不同的人，他们向人工智能聊天机器人询问了哪些问题。

资深记者

Rebecca Ruiz 是 Mashable 的高级记者。 她经常报道心理健康、数字文化和技术。 她的专业领域包括自杀预防、屏幕使用和心理健康、育儿、青少年福祉以及冥想和正念。 Rebecca 在加入 Mashable 之前的经历包括在 NBC News Digital 担任特约撰稿人、记者和编辑，以及在福布斯担任特约撰稿人。 丽贝卡拥有学士学位。 萨拉劳伦斯学院学士学位和加州大学硕士学位 伯克利新闻研究生院。

Mashable 最近委托 YouGov 进行的一项调查显示，大多数美国成年人都使用过 Claude 或 ChatGPT 等人工智能聊天机器人。 一般而言，我们甚至知道他们如何看待聊天机器人的助理、导师、顾问、治疗师和浪漫伴侣等角色，或者以上所有角色。

然而，这种用途的具体细节却更难掌握。

毕竟，人们不会在社交媒体平台和 Reddit 论坛之外深入了解聊天机器人的使用情况。 他们可能会感到羞耻或耻辱，因为他们把聊天机器人变成了他们的治疗师或配偶。 或者也许它不像《爱情岛》接管群聊那样成为对话的素材。

因此，Mashable 询问了三个截然不同的人——一位祖母、一位企业家和一位技术专家——他们如何使用人工智能聊天机器人。

他们的答案揭示了聊天机器人如何成为某些人的重要实用工具，即使他们仍在努力应对人工智能带来的更大的文化转变。

奶奶知道自己想从 ChatGPT 得到什么

去年秋天，71 岁的芭芭拉 (Barbara) 与她的儿子和儿媳合作，给 ChatGPT 一项艰巨的任务。 他们需要大型语言模型来帮助他们了解芭芭拉有学习障碍的孙子是否实现了学区设定的学习目标。

至关重要的是，如果学区对这个问题的回答是肯定的，他们可能会认为芭芭拉的孙子不再需要课堂支持。 她迫切地觉得他还是这么做的，他的父母也同意了。

芭芭拉向 Mashable 回忆道：“我们似乎从未得到过直接的答案，而且所说的内容也相互矛盾。” 为了保护孙子的隐私，她要求透露自己的名字。

在与学校工作人员就这个问题发生冲突的过程中，一家三口向聊天机器人求助。 芭芭拉（Barbara）曾是一名教育家，对一年两次的会议并不陌生，这些会议通常决定学生是否获得课堂支持以及程度。 但就连她也对她的孙子在小学多年积累的所有文件感到不知所措。

当然，还有成绩和考试成绩。 但她孙子的认知和智力也接受了地区和医疗专业人员的测试。 他们上传了所有文件并等待 ChatGPT 给出意见。

通过直接提示，该模型还考虑了该州的教育残疾法律和法规，以及教育部《残疾人教育法》手册的上传副本。 ChatGPT 最终站在芭芭拉及其家人一边。

Barbara 并不认为 ChatGPT 能返回一个确凿的证据或铁定的策略。 相反，她说聊天机器人的反馈让他们感觉为讨论她孙子的服务做好了更好的准备。 该家族还聘请了一名教育倡导者来帮助巩固他们的地位。 最终，芭芭拉的孙子保留了他的课堂服务。

"It's amazing to me, and kind of disturbing, because I really try not to tell it a lot about myself."

除了这项重要任务外，Barbara 告诉 Mashable，她还向 ChatGPT 寻求实用建议或产品比较。 她让聊天机器人为与朋友一起去爱尔兰的夏季旅行创建了一个行程；要求它识别出她喜欢的一款已停产的药店香水的仿冒品；并就她的机械师提议的价值 800 美元的汽车维修请求其建议。 ChatGPT 表示，补充她的本田 CRV 变速箱和制动液是合理的，但要避免使用高压机器冲洗变速箱等。

Barbara 在使用 ChatGPT 时避免的一件事是什么？ 像朋友或知己一样与它交谈，她觉得这“令人毛骨悚然”。

尽管如此，ChatGPT 对 Barbara 还是相当熟悉的。

“这对我来说很神奇，也有点令人不安，因为我真的尽量不透露太多关于我自己的事情，”她说。 “我努力让它保持高效，它对我的​​了解之多仍然令人惊讶。”

管理特工团队的人工智能人类学家

Matt Artz 是您可能在新闻文章或病毒式社交媒体帖子中读到过的人工智能用户类型。 他可以指挥克劳德特工团队在没有持续监督的情况下执行他的命令。 换句话说，他正在过着人工智能布道者所承诺的在不远的将来我们其他人也能过的生活。

但与许多 AI 用户相比，Artz 是独一无二的。 首先，他可以支付每月 200 美元的 Claude Max 订阅费用，这为他提供了比免费或较低级别订阅者更多的计算或处理能力。 因此，他说他在相同的时间内完成了更多的工作。

白天，他是一名人工智能产品经理。 40 多岁的 Artz 在业余时间正在攻读博士学位。 在计算人类学中。

因此，Artz 部署代理来执行任务就不足为奇了，例如根据他开发的风格指南构建个人网站；在提交之前审查和批评他的学术作品；并回填 200,000 篇人类学期刊文章的目录，以便它们的文献计量数据出现在维基数据中。 他以美国人类学协会董事会成员的身份承担了最后一个项目。

可混搭光速

同时，Artz 也清醒地认识到大型语言模型的局限性；他并不认为它们是绝对正确的。

因为它们的输出是概率性的，所以模型每次都可以以不同的方式处理相同的任务。 这就是为什么 Artz 有意为特工提供任何任务的详细结构和方向。 如果没有这一点，特工更有可能以他不希望的方式即兴发挥。 他还没有向特工丢失任何数据。

“它并不完美，”他告诉 Mashable。 “我认为当前的代理人工智能尚不适合执行超级敏感且必须 100% 准确的最高阶任务。”

不过，他指出，大多数知识工作都是主观的，这意味着一开始就很少有“正确”的答案。

Artz 也像普通人一样使用人工智能。 他要求克劳德根据客厅的布置选择一张沙发，并用不同的颜色渲染它的外观。 阿茨将多年的睡眠数据和观察结果上传给克劳德，以优化他的睡眠时间。

他说，克劳德帮助查明了一些变量，包括他从日记中记录的就寝时间的各个方面，最终使他平均每晚的深度睡眠时间延长了约 20 分钟。

不过，Artz 担心，一些人工智能用户没有意识到输出在多大程度上取决于他们质疑和反驳模型的能力。 那些不明白人工智能是概率性的人可能没有意识到他们可以反驳、改写问题，或者从相反的角度提出问题，看看答案是否成立。

此外，许多人可能没有意识到额外的计算可以产生更复杂和可靠的输出。

阿茨说，这些因素造成了“智力鸿沟”。

“你能支付多少情报，对吗？” 他问道。

换句话说，即使每个人都可以使用人工智能聊天机器人，结果也会根据你能负担得起的型号或订阅而有所不同。

反科技企业家

蔡斯·迪贝内代托

32 岁的拉里萨 (Larz) May 与屏幕有着复杂的关系。

她是一位著名的数字健康倡导者，也是“数字排毒”运动的早期先驱，受到她自己对社交媒体对心理健康危害的公众认识的推动。

她后来创立了#HalfTheStory，旨在在青少年和科技之间建立更好的关系。 梅解释道，该非营利组织为青少年和学校提供培训、指导和数字公民参与计划，并将年轻人置于人工智能安全对话的中心。 它促进了模拟聚会，例如无电话舞会。 梅甚至与希拉里·克林顿和纽约州州长合作。 凯西·霍楚尔 (Kathy Hochul) 制定了一项青少年引导的无电话学校政策，希望能鼓励全国范围内远离电子屏幕。

她还是 Ginko 的联合创始人，Ginko 是一种人工智能驱动的育儿工具，可以帮助家庭建立更健康的数字习惯并促进沟通。 她说，这款应用程序将屏幕时间变成了“通往现实世界的跳板”。

关键在于：梅可能是大型科技公司的直言不讳的批评者，但她绝对不是勒德分子。

"AI is an incredible sparring partner in the workplace."

“人工智能是工作场所中令人难以置信的陪练伙伴，”梅说。 她使用她认为不像克劳德那样阿谀奉承的聊天机器人来讨论想法或微调音调。 “我经常说，‘嘿，假装你是一位非常挑剔的首席营销官，然后把这件事撕碎。’”

她还使用 Granola（一种人工智能笔记记录器和会议合成器）和 Wispr Flow（一种人工智能，可以让她口述自己的想法并将其转化为文本）。

梅说她理解为什么年轻人转向聊天机器人寻求支持。 新冠疫情后的世界让许多早期职业专业人士和应届毕业生失去了工作场所的联系或指导。 充满冲突的新闻周期和错误信息加剧了普遍的疲劳，使您很容易转向可以清晰而友善地与您交谈的答案引擎。 梅发现自己在感到精疲力竭时也更加依赖聊天机器人。

她说，对许多人来说，社交媒体就像一个需要不断表演的舞台。 人工智能聊天机器人可以显示为更私密的空间。

“聊天机器人就像一个休息室，”梅解释道。 “人工智能是年轻人趋向的软角落，因为世界非常艰难，而且我们正在经历如此多的变化。”

但梅也对科技的负面影响有着亲身经历。 她说，聊天机器人无法取代人类的发明、联系和批判性思维能力。 她看到人们很容易迷恋人工智能，从而带来巨大的潜在危害，并对大型科技公司的动机提出质疑。

“社交媒体破坏了我们的多巴胺，”梅说。 “但人工智能在很多方面正在侵入我们的催产素——人类的联系激素。”

梅仍然主张断开连接，但这在人工智能时代意味着不同的东西。

“这不再是科技时代了。 更重要的是你不接触科技的时代，”她建议道。 “就像 10 年前我会说每周有一天禁食社交媒体一样，现在更重要的是实际上每周有一天而不是在工作中使用人工智能。 看看你对它的依赖程度，这样你就知道你可能会失去多少认知能力。”

她说，如果我们的职业、教育，甚至我们的生活就像我们驾驶的汽车，那么我们就必须将人工智能视为 GPS。 聊天机器人提供了一些路径，你最终可以选择不走这些路径。 它们不是引擎。

“你应该坐在驾驶座上，”梅警告说。 “你应该告诉人工智能你希望它成为谁，批评你正在做的事情，而不是相反。 如果没有，人工智能就会驱动你。”
